Package io.thymekit

Class ElementContract

java.lang.Object
io.thymekit.ElementContract
public final class ElementContract extends Object
The walk over a triple, handed to whoever writes an element. The kit checks its own elements with it; an element of yours is checked the same way, in your own test: 

 @Test
 void myElementsKeepTheContract() {
     ElementContract.of(Price.of("12.00", "EUR"), Badge.of("in stock"))
         .renderedBy(templateEngine)
         .styledBy("static/my/ui.css")
         .check();
 }

What it looks at is what no compiler can: that the address points at a fragment that exists and declares itself, that the adapter is named the way an adapter is named, that a script has not been put where an element belongs, and — when an engine and stylesheets are given — that the element renders something, and that every class it prints has a rule somewhere in the CSS you name.

Nothing here is required to write an element. It is the same walk the kit takes over its own, and it fails with every problem at once rather than with the first.

    • templatesUnder

      public ElementContract templatesUnder(String... classpathPrefixes)
      Where your templates live on the classpath, when they are not under templates/ — the prefix your template resolver was given, "views/" or whatever it is. Without this the contract looks under templates/ and then at the address as written, which covers the default and nothing else.

    • styledBy

      public ElementContract styledBy(String... cssResources)
      Where the looks live, as classpath resources ("static/my/ui.css"). Given these, every class an element prints must have a rule in one of them; without them the classes are not looked at, since the contract has no way to guess where a consumer keeps its CSS.

    • check

      public void check()
      Runs the walk. Throws with everything that is wrong, not with the first thing.
